title: 500 people vibe-coded for 30 days. I was one of them. - Sanja Grbic, Automattic

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on how a designer collaborated with AI coding tools to transform her role and workflow, emphasizing human collaboration, organizational enablement, and process change rather than the technical system itself. The experiment occurred within Automattic's internal enterprise operations and used coding assistant tooling to enable non-engineers to ship software. The talk traces projects from initial ideation through prototyping, development, and deployment to production. The presentation is a first-person narrative with no technical prerequisites, accessible to any audience. The talk is a personal case study of three projects built during a 30-day organizational experiment. All evidence anchors are direct quotes graded as said_in_transcript.

summary: Sanja Grbic, a product designer with 5 years at Automattic and over a decade of experience, presents her experience in Radical Speed Month, a 30-day experiment where two-person teams were given full autonomy to build and ship projects while pausing the roadmap. Automattic, behind WordPress.com, Jetpack, WooCommerce, Tumblr, and Beeper, has about 1,400 people in a fully distributed, asynchronous setup with extensive accumulated documentation. Approximately 500 people participated in the first round, starting 794 projects. Before the experiment, Automattic invested in AI enablement through tools, courses, a two-week immersive role-specific training program, and infrastructure support so non-engineers could spin up development environments. A key tool is Context AC, an MCP server giving AI tools access to company knowledge. Sanja built three projects. First, during AI enablement training, a group of four (two designers, one engineer, one product lead) built a board game session manager in two hours using Claude Code. The engineer set up GitHub and taught Git basics, leading to Sanja's insight that engineers should become enablers and teachers. Second, her main project was a design system status tracker built over 2.5 weeks. After initial discovery with an engineer and design ops person, she built the full proof of concept solo, pulling links from GitHub, Storybook, and Figma, sorting by status and tagging with library names. This marked her transition from designer to design engineer, meaning pushing code to production in a well-established large system requiring serious onboarding and security practices. Third, in just 6 days, she paired with another designer to build an iOS chat for WooCommerce merchants with authentication, Jetpack connection, a site-themed widget, and an AI agent answering visitor questions. The two designers aligned easily on features because both always had users in mind. They started exploration as a Claude Code project folder where chats and ideas were recorded into a file system, significantly speeding up collaboration and the later build. The biggest process shift was using the prototype as the main artifact: instead of starting in Figma and working to high fidelity, they planned, built the prototype, then returned to Figma only for a visual mood board and UI fine-tuning. In 30 days, Sanja's process completely shifted, and this was true for many other participants. She advises large organizations to implement similar experiments at the team level by providing access to tools, finding enablers and champions, creating space for experimentation, and giving people agency to break habits and unlock the speed AI tools can bring.

takeaways: AI tools and full process ownership enabled a designer to ship production-quality software independently, transitioning to a design engineer role capable of pushing code to production in a large established system.
Engineers can have greater impact by enabling and teaching others rather than solely doing engineering themselves.
Full autonomy eliminates handover bottlenecks common in large organizations, dramatically accelerating shipping velocity.
Radical Speed Month demonstrated that pausing roadmap work for 30 days can unlock significant output across a large distributed company.
Prior investment in AI enablement training and infrastructure was critical to enabling non-engineers to contribute in code.
Starting exploration as a Claude Code project folder with recorded chats and ideas sped up collaboration and the later build.
The biggest process shift was prototyping directly in code, using Figma only afterward for visual mood boards and UI fine-tuning rather than starting in Figma.
Large organizations should provide tool access, find enablers and champions, create experimentation space, and give people agency to break habits and unlock AI-driven speed.
Engineers need to become enablers and teachers in mixed-ability teams

sections.title: Introduction and Automattic Context
sections.summary: Sanja introduces herself and Automattic, describing the company's products, fully distributed asynchronous structure, and her decade of experience. She frames AI as a new versatile tool expected to bring speed, noting velocity differs between small teams and large organizations.

sections.title: AI Enablement at Automattic
sections.summary: Describes Automattic's progressive AI adoption: tools and courses, a two-week immersive role-specific AI enablement training, infrastructure enabling non-engineers to spin up dev environments, and Context AC MCP server for accessing accumulated company knowledge.

sections.title: Radical Speed Month Overview
sections.summary: Explains the experiment: pause roadmap for 30 days, pair with a partner, ship something real. About 500 people started 794 projects. Sanja built three projects while also attending in-person AI enablement training, having never before built and shipped code at work.

sections.title: Project 1: Board Game Session Manager
sections.summary: Built in 2 hours during AI training by a group of four using Claude Code. The engineer set up GitHub and taught Git basics. Key learning: engineers should become enablers and teachers, with impact potentially greater than doing engineering themselves.

sections.title: Project 2: Design System Status Tracker
sections.summary: Main project built over 2.5 weeks to surface design system information. Sanja built the full proof of concept solo, pulling from GitHub, Storybook, and Figma. This marked her transition from designer to design engineer, enabled by full ownership without handover negotiations.

sections.title: Project 3: iOS Chat for WooCommerce Merchants
sections.summary: Built in 6 days with a fellow designer. Full proof of concept with wordpress.com authentication, Jetpack connection, site-themed widget, and AI agent answering visitor questions. Demonstrates a dramatic shift in speed and process.

sections.title: Process Shifts and Recommendations
sections.summary: Sanja reflects on the process changes from the third project: two designers aligned easily on features, started exploration in a Claude Code project folder recording chats and ideas, and used the prototype as the main artifact—building in code first, then returning to Figma only for visual mood boards and UI fine-tuning. Her process shifted completely in 30 days, as it did for many others. She summarizes the three projects' lessons and advises large organizations to provide tool access, find enablers and champions, create experimentation space, and give people agency to break habits and unlock AI-driven speed.
